result: The unc-119 mutant ed3 exhibits fully penetrant microtubule orientation defects in the PVD anterior dendrite and occasionally in axons, with similar phenotypes observed in PHC neurons but not in ciliated URX and PQR neurons. The mutant also shows synaptic vesicle mislocalization and morphological defects including shorter axons/dendrites and reduced branching, resembling defects in unc-33 and unc-44 mutants.
evaluation: Claims C1-C9 are well-supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B-E and supplementary figures. The microtubule orientation defects are quantified with appropriate controls, and the phenotypic similarities to unc-33 and unc-44 mutants are supported by both current data and citations to previous work. The observation that ciliated neurons are unaffected is consistent with prior knowledge about alternative microtubule organization mechanisms in these cells.

result: unc-119 is mainly expressed in neurons and codes for a highly conserved protein homologous to human UNC119A/B. PVD-specific expression of UNC-119::GFP rescues the dendritic microtubule defect, indicating cell-intrinsic function, though the molecular mechanism remains unknown.
evaluation: Claims C10-C13 are supported by rescue experiments (Figure 1C) and citations to established literature. The cell-intrinsic function is appropriately inferred from the cell-specific rescue. Claim C14 accurately represents the knowledge gap that motivates the study.

result: UNC-119::GFP knock-in animals show strongest expression in neurons with low levels in non-neuronal cells. The fusion protein is functional (normal locomotion) and shows 70-80% immobile fraction in axons and dendrites by FRAP, suggesting tight association with undefined structures important for neuronal development and microtubule organization.
evaluation: Claims C15-C22 are well-supported by imaging data (Figure 1F) and FRAP experiments (Figure 1G-I). The functionality of the fusion protein is appropriately inferred from normal locomotion. The high immobile fraction is quantified and supports the conclusion of tight association with cellular structures. The inference about importance for neuronal development is supported by the mutant phenotypes.

result: UNC-33 (CRMP) was identified as a top-scoring interaction partner of UNC-119 by immunoprecipitation/mass spectrometry. UNC-33 is a putative microtubule binding protein with three isoforms (S, M, L), where only UNC-33L rescues neuronal polarity defects. Mutations in unc-33 produce similar microtubule defects as unc-119.
evaluation: Claims C23-C28 are supported by mass spectrometry data (Supplementary file 1) and citations to previous work. The identification of UNC-33 as an interaction partner is data-driven. The characterization of isoforms and their differential rescue capacity is well-established in cited literature. The phenotypic similarity between mutants is supported by both current and previous data.

result: UNC-33L (but not UNC-33S) efficiently binds UNC-119 via its N-terminus in pull-down experiments. UNC-119 bridges UNC-44 to UNC-33, as UNC-44 C-terminus binds UNC-119, and UNC-33L only binds UNC-44 in UNC-119's presence, forming a ternary complex. The three proteins have similar mutant phenotypes, suggesting common function in neuronal development.
evaluation: Claims C29-C41 are well-supported by systematic pull-down experiments in Hek293T cells (Figure 2A-D) and yeast two-hybrid data from literature. The ternary complex formation is demonstrated through appropriate controls showing UNC-33L requires UNC-119 to bind UNC-44. The inference of common function is reasonable given similar phenotypes and complex formation.

result: UNC-44::GFP (giant AO13 Ankyrin isoform) localizes to axons, dendrites, and cortex with expression pattern similar to UNC-119::GFP. It is highly immobile by FRAP (as expected for cortical cytoskeleton proteins), and this immobility is independent of UNC-119 or UNC-33, indicating UNC-44 acts upstream.
evaluation: Claims C42-C49 are supported by GFP knock-in imaging (Figure 3B-C) and FRAP experiments (Figure 3D-H). The cortical localization is clearly shown. The independence of UNC-44 immobility from UNC-119/UNC-33 is demonstrated in mutant backgrounds, appropriately supporting the upstream position inference. The expectation of immobility for cortical cytoskeleton proteins is well-cited.

result: UNC-119 recovers rapidly and diffuses freely in the unc-44 mutant, while its immobility is unaffected in the unc-33 mutant, suggesting UNC-44 binds and stabilizes UNC-119.
evaluation: Claims C50-C52 are supported by FRAP experiments in mutant backgrounds (Figure 3I-J). The differential behavior in unc-44 vs unc-33 mutants provides strong evidence for the proposed relationship. The inference that UNC-44 stabilizes UNC-119 is appropriately drawn from the mobility changes.

result: UNC-33L specifically rescues microtubule orientation defects when expressed in PVD neurons. FRAP analysis shows UNC-33L has ~85% immobile fraction while UNC-33M/S have ~60%, suggesting the smaller isoforms have both diffusing and anchored pools. UNC-33L immobility is lost in unc-44 or unc-119 mutants, indicating UNC-44 immobilizes UNC-33L via UNC-119.
evaluation: Claims C53-C61 are well-supported by rescue experiments (Figure 3M) and FRAP analysis (Figure 3N-T). The differential immobility between isoforms is quantified. The dependence of UNC-33L immobility on UNC-44 and UNC-119 is demonstrated in appropriate mutant backgrounds. The hierarchical relationship is appropriately inferred from the dependency data.

result: UNC-44 (Ankyrin), UNC-119, and UNC-33L all show ~180-200 nm periodic patterns by TIRF-SIM, similar to β-spectrin (UNC-70), while UNC-33M lacks periodicity. The ternary complex shares a stereotypic periodic pattern similar to the cortical spectrin cytoskeleton.
evaluation: Claims C62-C68 are supported by TIRF-SIM imaging data (Figure 4A-E) with appropriate statistical analysis (Wilcoxon rank sum tests). The periodicity measurements are quantified and compared across proteins. The lack of periodicity for UNC-33M is consistent with its inability to bind UNC-119. The inference about similarity to spectrin cytoskeleton is well-supported by the data and established knowledge.

result: Both UNC-33S and UNC-33L efficiently bind microtubules via their C-terminus when expressed in hypodermal seam cells. Upon loss of microtubule binding, UNC-33L (but not UNC-33S) partially relocalizes to the cortex in a UNC-44 and UNC-119 dependent manner.
evaluation: Claims C69-C73 are supported by ectopic expression experiments in seam cells (Figure 5A-B) and established literature about CRMP microtubule binding. The differential cortical relocalization between UNC-33L and UNC-33S upon C-terminus deletion is clearly demonstrated, and the dependence on UNC-44/UNC-119 is shown in mutant backgrounds.

result: FRAP analysis shows UNC-33S/MΔC rapidly recover, indicating their immobile pool results from microtubule binding. However, UNC-33LΔC remains highly immobile despite lacking the C-terminus, though C-terminus binding is essential for function. UNC-33LΔC becomes mobile in unc-119 mutants, showing UNC-119 binds the N-terminus to immobilize UNC-33L to UNC-44. Thus, UNC-33L associates with microtubules via its C-terminus and cortex via N-terminal UNC-119 interaction.
evaluation: Claims C74-C81 are well-supported by systematic FRAP experiments with deletion constructs (Figure 5C-K). The differential behavior of ΔC constructs between isoforms is clearly demonstrated. The requirement for C-terminus function is shown by rescue experiments. The N-terminal interaction with UNC-119 is demonstrated by mobility changes in unc-119 mutants. The overall model is appropriately inferred from the combined data.

result: The UNC-44/119/33 complex anchors microtubules in neurons. In wild type, microtubules are evenly distributed and largely immobile in mature neurons. In unc-44, unc-119, and unc-33 mutants, microtubules penetrate side branches, show increased mobility and buckling, and the photoactivated tubulin region translocates (biased toward cell body), demonstrating the complex functions as a cortical anchoring complex.
evaluation: Claims C82-C90 are strongly supported by MAPH-1 imaging (Figure 6A-B) and photoactivation experiments (Figure 6C-E). The loss of microtubule immobility in all three mutants provides compelling evidence for the anchoring function. The quantification of microtubule sliding with directional bias is well-documented. The inference about cortical anchoring function is appropriately drawn from the combined data.

result: Loss of unc-116 (kinesin-1) or klc-2 (kinesin light chain) completely suppresses microtubule mobility in unc-33 mutants but not polarity or morphology defects. Loss of unc-104 (kinesin-3) does not suppress mobility. This shows kinesin-1 specifically slides microtubules in the absence of cortical anchoring, and the complex acts to curb kinesin-1 activity for proper neuronal development.
evaluation: Claims C91-C98 are well-supported by photoactivation experiments in double mutants (Figure 7A-C). The specificity for kinesin-1 is demonstrated by the lack of suppression with unc-104 depletion. The suppression of mobility but not polarity defects is clearly shown. The proposed model about balancing kinesin-1 activity is appropriately inferred from the genetic interaction data, though it remains somewhat speculative.

result: Artificial coupling of UNC-33S to UNC-44 (via vhhGFP nanobody) rescues microtubule defects and neuronal morphology in unc-33 and unc-119 mutants. Pan-neuronal expression rescues locomotion in unc-119 mutants, demonstrating the locomotion defect is caused by loss of UNC-33L anchoring to cortical UNC-44.
evaluation: Claims C99-C102 are strongly supported by rescue experiments using the artificial tethering approach (Figure 8B-E). This is a critical experiment that validates the proposed model by bypassing UNC-119. The rescue of microtubule organization, morphology, and locomotion provides compelling evidence that the primary function of UNC-119 is to anchor UNC-33 to UNC-44. The inference about causation is appropriately drawn from the rescue data.

result: The unc-119 mutant is severely paralyzed and has been used as a transgenesis background. While unc-119 expression in neurons and importance for development are known, the molecular function was unknown. This study shows UNC-119 is part of a membrane-anchored complex that anchors microtubules, and depletion leads to kinesin-1-induced microtubule sliding, which is the underlying cause of polarity defects and impaired development.
evaluation: Claims C103-C109 appropriately summarize the study's context and main findings. The prior knowledge claims are well-cited. The new findings about UNC-119 function are supported by the experimental data. However, claim C109 about excessive sliding being the "underlying cause" is somewhat speculative, as the exact mechanism linking sliding to polarity defects is not fully demonstrated.

result: Neuronal development relies on a balance between kinesin-1-dependent microtubule sliding and cortical anchoring. This balance is important across organisms. In Drosophila, kinesin-1 has an additional microtubule binding site for sliding. In C. elegans, mutating this site reduces minus-end-out organization. While Drosophila kinesin-1 sliding is supposedly KLC-independent, C. elegans KLC-2 depletion suppresses sliding in unc-33 mutants.
evaluation: Claims C110-C118 integrate current findings with established literature. The citations to prior work are appropriate. The observation that KLC-2 depletion suppresses sliding (C118) is supported by experimental data (Figure 7), which contrasts with Drosophila findings and represents a novel contribution. The overall model about balance is well-supported but remains somewhat conceptual.

result: UNC-119 is highly conserved and important for neuronal development across species, but the mechanism was unknown. Mammalian UNC119 binds myristoylated proteins and acts as a chaperone, with Arl2/3 releasing cargo. C. elegans UNC-119 interacts with Arl2/3 and affects ciliary transport, but Arl2/3 mutants lack microtubule defects. Direct attachment of UNC-33 to UNC-44 rescues unc-119 mutants, demonstrating UNC-119 functions as a structural scaffold.
evaluation: Claims C119-C131 appropriately discuss the relationship between the current findings and established UNC119 functions. The citations to prior work are appropriate. The key observation that Arl2/3 mutants lack microtubule defects (C129) distinguishes the scaffolding function from the chaperone function. The rescue by direct tethering (C130) strongly supports the scaffolding model. The inference about structural scaffold function (C131) is well-supported.

result: Microtubule stabilization mechanisms vary across organisms. In Drosophila, MKLP1 counteracts kinesin-1 and Shot stabilizes microtubules. In mammals, various MAPs stabilize microtubules. Giant Ankyrin isoforms connect submembrane cytoskeleton to microtubules differently across species. In C. elegans, UNC-44 interacts with microtubules via UNC-119/UNC-33. The complex might function similarly in other species, though UNC-119 binds the non-conserved UNC-33L N-terminus, requiring further research.
evaluation: Claims C132-C144 appropriately discuss evolutionary conservation and species differences. The citations are appropriate. The observation that UNC-119 binds the non-conserved N-terminus (C144) is important for understanding potential species differences. The speculation about conservation (C143) is appropriately cautious given the sequence differences. This represents thoughtful discussion rather than overinterpretation.

result: Mature neuronal microtubules are largely immobile, but during development, neurite growth/retraction is linked to microtubule dynamics, suggesting the anchoring complex or microtubule binding is regulated. CRMP hyperphosphorylation in Alzheimer's disease and Ankyrin-B mutations in autism affect microtubule organization, suggesting conserved mechanisms. Understanding neuronal microtubule connections may help treat damaged neurons.
evaluation: Claims C145-C153 appropriately discuss developmental regulation and disease relevance. The observations about microtubule immobility are supported by current and cited data. The speculation about regulation (C147) is reasonable given developmental dynamics. The disease connections (C148-C151) are appropriately cited. The inference about conservation (C152) is supported by cross-species similarities. The therapeutic speculation (C153) is appropriately cautious.

result: While the microtubule cytoskeleton's central role in neuronal polarity is known, how its organization is established and maintained is poorly understood. This study shows UNC-119 links membrane-associated UNC-44 to microtubule-associated UNC-33, forming a periodic complex that anchors microtubule bundles to oppose kinesin-1 sliding. Disturbing this complex alters polarity and causes severe developmental defects and paralysis.
evaluation: Claims C154-C159 provide an appropriate summary of the study's context and main findings. The knowledge gap (C154-C155) is accurately stated. The main findings (C156-C158) are well-supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript. The consequences of disrupting the complex (C159) are clearly demonstrated by the mutant phenotypes.

result: Axons have plus-end-out microtubules while dendrites have mixed (vertebrates) or minus-end-out (invertebrates) organization, allowing selective cargo transport and representing an evolutionarily conserved polarity characteristic. Disorganized microtubules cause transport and polarity defects and are associated with neuronal diseases and regeneration capacity. During development, microtubules are mobile and can be transported by kinesin-1 through sliding. Later, microtubules are immobilized by MAPs and cortical connections. The balance between kinesin-1 sliding and cortical anchoring is essential for neuronal development.
evaluation: Claims C160-C174 provide appropriate background context with well-cited established knowledge. The integration of prior work with current findings is appropriate. The proposed model about balance (C174) is supported by the experimental data, though it remains somewhat conceptual. This represents a well-supported synthesis of the field.
